title: The History of Mentos — They Made a Soda Fountain and Became Famous for Free
fullText: In 2006, two street performers carried out an experiment that exploded across the internet, both literally and figuratively at the same time. They lined up dozens of bottles of soda, dropped several pieces of candy into each one, and fountains shot several meters into the air, one after another, just like real geysers in a synchronized show. The video spread around the world before the familiar concept of a viral video even existed in the way we understand it today. The company that produced those candies had absolutely nothing to do with the experiment itself. No one paid the two performers a single scent. No one coordinated the use of the brand with them. And there was no marketing department standing behind the scenes. And yet this completely accidental independently created video became one of the most successful marketing stories in the entire history of the confectionary industry simply because the company noticed what was happening around its own product at exactly the right moment and decided not to interfere but to embrace it. At the same time, far less harmless rumors began spreading across America that eating the same candy together with an ordinary soft drink was deadly dangerous to your health. Concerned parents forbade their children from combining the two. Some schools introduced official bans in their cafeterias and popular science programs were forced to investigate the issue on air, separating objective scientific fact from an ordinary wave of public panic. How did an ordinary mint candy from a small Dutch company become the main character in one of the most famous home experiments in internet history? Why did a company that paid absolutely nothing to create this phenomenon ultimately earn more from it than from decades of traditional advertising? And is it really true that combining this candy with soda can actually be dangerous? The history of Mentos begins in 1932 in the small Dutch city of Brada, where the local family-owned company Vonmemell, which had already spent several decades producing chewing gum and a variety of other confectionary products in its own modest manufacturing facilities, introduced a new mint candy with a firm, chewy texture and a distinctive, strongly refreshing mint flavor. The product was originally conceived as a relatively modest local addition to the company's existing product range with no particular ambitions for widespread international success during the first few decades of its existence on the Dutch market. The candy's production technology was considered relatively innovative for its time. Its dense, slightly chewy texture was achieved through a specialized process for treating the sugar mass. While its distinctive round shape with a small indentation on top became a recognizable visual feature of the brand for decades to come. Throughout the 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s, Mentos remained primarily a regional product known mainly in the company's home country of the Netherlands and in several neighboring European countries, where the candy gradually spread through local distributors and confectionary wholesalers. Nothing during this relatively quiet period in the company's history suggested that just a few decades later, this modest mint candy from a provincial Dutch town would become a recognizable international brand, let alone the star of one of the most widely discussed science entertainment phenomena in the history of the internet, which at that point in history did not yet exist in the familiar form we know today. and in practical terms could not have existed at all. The real breakthrough in the brand's international recognition came in the 1990s when von Mel launched a largecale and genuinely memorable advertising campaign built around the concise slogan the freshmaker. The format of the commercials proved so successful, instantly recognizable and adaptable across different cultural contexts that the company continued using it for several decades with almost no fundamental changes to its structure. The main character in each commercial inevitably finds himself in an awkward, embarrassing, or openly absurd everyday situation. trapped in a suddenly stalled elevator, caught in a comically tense and uncomfortable social situation at work or on public transportation, and then calmly pulls out the distinctive Mentos package from his pocket, eats a single candy, and suddenly finds an effortless way out of the difficult situation, demonstrating unexpected ingenuity and complete, almost icy composure at a moment when almost anyone else would probably have panicked. This simple in structure but highly effective advertising formula helped the brand move far beyond its native Netherlands and begin a genuinely active international expansion into dozens of foreign markets including the United States where the company started systematically promoting the product through television commercials in the same recognizable light-hearted and comedic style that had already proven successful across Europe. European markets. By the end of the 1990s, Mentos had firmly established itself as a genuinely recognizable international confectionary brand, widely available on storeshelves almost all over the world. Although at that point it was still far from being among the absolute leaders of the global mint candy and chewing gum market, lagging significantly behind several larger and more established competitors in overall sales volume. In 2001, an important corporate event took place that permanently changed the ownership structure of the brand, but went almost completely unnoticed by the ordinary consumer, who continued buying the familiar candy at the supermarket checkout. The Dutch company Van Mel merged with the major Italian confectionary company Perfetti, forming a new combined corporation called Perfetti Vanmel. By that point in history, the Italian side of the merger already owned its own extensive portfolio of international confectionary brands, including a number of recognizable chewing gum and candy labels. And the combination of the two historically independent companies created one of the largest private confectionary manufacturers in the world with production and distribution on a scale capable of competing with such established giants of the global industry as Mars and Mandles. A telling detail that few people ever think about while casually eating another piece of candy on the go. Despite the enormous scale of the combined corporation, which today sells its products in more than 150 countries around the world and operates dozens of manufacturing facilities across different continents, Herfetti Van Mel remains entirely privately owned and even more unusually for a business of such impressive size in the modern global economy is still fully controlled by a single Italian family, the Lang family who rarely appear in public and almost never give extensive interviews to the press about the internal structure of their business or the personal details of how they manage the company. This is a characteristic and fairly common feature of a number of large family-owned confectionary empires around the world, which prefer to remain in theformational shadow of their far more recognizable consumer brands for generations, rarely placing themselves personally at the center of public attention. In 2006, two street performers from the state of Maine, Fritz Grobe and Steven Vultz, known together under the creative name Epie Bird and previously making their living through street circus performances and juggling recorded an experimental video that would permanently enter the history of internet culture. The idea behind the experiment was extremely simple to describe. If several Mentos mint candies are drugged into a bottle of Diet Coke, a violent physical reaction takes place, causing a powerful fountain of carbonated foam to burst out of the neck of the bottle with a whistle and characteristic hiss shooting several meters into the air just seconds after the candies come into contact with the liquid. The pair, drawing on their many years of experience staging visually spectacular circus performances, built an elaborate composition involving 101 bottles of Diet Coke, synchronously released Mentos candies into each bottle using a homemade mechanical device, and filmed the resulting spectacle in a single long take. An impressive cascade of fountains erupting one after another in a precisely calculated rhythm resembling a choreographed stage performance or a kind of water ballet made of foam and sugar. The video was uploaded to YouTube, a relatively young video platform at the time that had barely existed for a single year when the footage was published. And it almost immediately began attracting an enormous number of views, spreading across the internet at a speed virtually unprecedented for that era when the very concept of a viral video had not yet fully taken shape in the public consciousness or acquired an established name. An important detail worth emphasizing separately. Neither Perfetti Van Mel nor the manufacturer of Diet Coke played any role whatsoever in creating this video and neither even knew of its existence until it was officially published online. It was a completely organic and entirely independent creative experiment by two private individuals with no contractual or commercial connection whatsoever to the official marketing of either of the two recognizable brands that happened to find themselves at the center of public attention because of the video. The success of Epie Bird's first video triggered a genuine wave of imitations across the internet. Thousands of ordinary users around the world, inspired by the original footage, began filming their own amateur versions of the Mentos and Soda Fountain experiment in their backyards and garages, trying to surpass the original in the scale of the production, the total number of bottles involved, or the creativity of the visual design. The phenomenon quickly moved far beyond simple backyard experiments. The popular science television show Mythbusters devoted an entire episode to a detailed examination of the true physical nature of the spectacular reaction, clearly explaining to millions of viewers that the explosive effect is not caused by any chemical reaction between the substances themselves, but by a purely physical process known in science as nucleation. The rough, porous surface of the candy creates countless microscopic nucleation sites around which the carbon dioxide dissolved in the drink is released almost instantly and simultaneously in the form of millions of tiny bubbles. The creators of the original video, Grobe and Volultz, unexpectedly became recognizable internet celebrities, first on a regional level and then across the entire country. and over the following years began staging increasingly large and technically complex Mentos fountain performances on live television shows, including David Letterman's famous late night talk show where they demonstrated before an astonished studio audience a working setup consisting of several hundred Diet Coke bottles triggered simultaneously through an elaborate mechanical release system. At the same time, alongside their public appearances, the pair set and repeatedly updated their own Guinness World Records for the number of soda bottles used simultaneously in a single performance. Each new attempt generating another wave of media attention around a phenomenon that had originally been nothing more than an accident and an amateur creative experiment by two street performers rather than the result of any deliberate marketing strategy. By their hundth and later videos, the pair were already deliberately experimenting with the shapes of the fountains themselves, adding elements of synchronized movement between the streams, and even testing different types of soda in order to achieve the most visually spectacular effect possible for each new production. At the same time, as the phenomenon grew in popularity as a purely entertaining spectacle, far more alarming rumors began spreading online. rumors that were not originally connected in any way to the harmless experiment involving bottles of soda. Through social networks, school hallways, and ordinary word of mouth, a story began circulating that if a person ate a Mentos candy and almost immediately drank a carbonated beverage, the same violent reaction could theoretically occur inside their own stomach, potentially causing serious internal injuries or even death. As these stories were retold, they accumulated more and more dramatic details. And some versions of the rumors even attributed specific, though never officially documented or confirmed, deaths among children and teenagers in different parts of the country to such hypothetical incidents. The public panic became serious and widespread enough to directly affect the everyday lives of ordinary school children. Some American schools officially banned students from bringing Mentos candies into the cafeteria together with any carbonated drinks. Concerned parents began demanding official explanations directly from the manufacturers. And Perfetti Vanelli itself was forced to publicly address the situation and officially reassure the public that its product was safe when consumed normally and responsibly. scientists, specialized popular science publications, and even the already mentioned television show Mythbusters quickly began explaining the key physical difference between the two situations to a mass audience. Inside a sealed glass or plastic bottle, dissolved carbon dioxide is released almost instantly and with considerable mechanical force because the gas is under pressure and has essentially nowhere to escape except through the bottle's narrow opening. Whereas inside the human stomach, the same process occurs far slowly and gradually while the body is naturally capable of releasing excess gas long before any truly dangerous level of internal pressure could build up. Nevertheless, the very fact that such an urban legend was able to spread so widely across the country and create real tangible public concern, reaching school cafeterias, parent committees, and even local television news broadcasts clearly demonstrates just how powerful, unpredictable, and at times potentially harmful in its wider social effects the cultural impact of an originally completely harmless amateur soda fountain experiment turned out to be. The experiment had been conceived by two street performers purely as a visually spectacular piece of entertainment. [music] Yet, its influence eventually extended far beyond the original video itself. Interestingly, urban legends surrounding perfectly ordinary food products are not particularly rare in the history of popular culture. But not every one of them ends up receiving a dedicated investigation on national television involving professional engineers and scientists patiently explaining the basic physics of the process to millions of concerned viewers. watching the truly unprecedented organic success of a phenomenon that brought the Mentos brand far more free public attention and recognition than entire decades of traditional television advertising could have generated. The leadership of Propheti Van Mel made a deliberate strategic decision not to fight the already uncontrollable spread of the video across the internet, but on the contrary to support it as much as possible and officially take the lead in the phenomenon's further development. The company began working directly with Grobe and Voltz, officially providing financial sponsorship for their subsequent increasingly ambitious and technically complex productions, as well as their regular record attempts instead of trying to distance itself from the unexpectedly emerging phenomenon or even more so taking legal action against the creators of the original video for using its brand without authorization for entertainment purposes. This particular case is now frequently cited by marketing professors and business writers as one of the earliest and most illustrative historical examples of what would later become widely known throughout the professional marketing industry as user generated content. And all of this happened long before the concept itself had fully developed into a distinct discipline within digital marketing. Complete with its own terminology, methodology, and established professional practices now taught in business schools around the world. Perfetti Van Mel effectively received one of the most recognizable, widely discussed, and genuinely memorable viral marketing phenomena of the early 2000s, completely free of charge without spending a single advertising dollar on its original creation. The company then demonstrated enough marketing flexibility, awareness, and strategic foresight to recognize the real commercial value of what was happening around its own product at [music] exactly the right moment and successfully integrate this accidental phenomenon into the brand's official communication strategy for many years to come. Significantly outperforming most of its industry competitors in this respect at the time. So, what ultimately came out of the story of a modest mint candy from a small Dutch city? A product that originally had no serious ambitions for widespread international recognition beyond its native Netherlands. A product that had spent many decades living largely in the shadow of far bigger and more recognizable competitors in the global confectionary market was suddenly transformed thanks to a completely accidental creative experiment by two street performers from the small American state of Maine who had no connection whatsoever to the company itself into one of the most recognizable symbols of the early age of internet virality. And this happened even before the very concept of viral content had fully taken shape in the form we know today or acquired a widely established name in popular culture. At the same time, the very same story unexpectedly produced a far less harmless side effect, a widely spread urban legend about the supposedly deadly danger of combining an innocent mint candy with an ordinary carbonated drink. The rumor became widespread enough to prompt real American schools to introduce official restrictions in their cafeterias, concerned parents to write letters to manufacturers, and a major international corporation to publicly and patiently explain the simple physics behind the process to a broad audience through the mass media. And perhaps the most revealing and genuinely instructive part of this entire story is that when a large international confectionary corporation unexpectedly found itself confronted with a completely uncontrollable viral phenomenon surrounding its own product, it ultimately made the conscious decision not to fight it, but to embrace it and officially take the lead. In doing so, the company transformed what was essentially the independent, unsolicited creative work of two street performers into one of the most effective and genuinely memorable marketing stories in its entire corporate history. And it did so long before such a strategy had even acquired an official name in modern digital marketing textbooks. So, the next time you unwrap a roll of ordinary Mentos mints on your way to work, remember this modest little candy once accidentally became part of one of the most famous experiments in the history of the internet and at the same time unintentionally became the star of one of the most persistent and longlasting urban legends of the early 21st century.
